inventory.name: Traveler's Pack
inventory.description: A worn canvas pack with good straps — bedroll, flint, mess kit, fifty small comforts of the road.

inventory.name: Waterskin
inventory.description: Boiled and refilled at the last clean spring. Worth more every week the river runs gray.

inventory.name: Belt Knife
inventory.description: A plain working blade — more tool than weapon, but it has been both.

inventory.name: Hemp Rope (30 ft)
inventory.description: Tarred hemp, knotted every arm's length. The difference between a fall and a climb.

inventory.name: Dried Rations
inventory.description: Fish, fruit leather, hard bread. Two days if you're honest with yourself, three if you're not.

inventory.name: Loose Paving-Stone
inventory.description: A flat grey stone worked loose from an Edge District light-guide street, threaded with faint mineral veining. Stowed to complete the test errand.

inventory.name: Loose Paving-Stones x2
inventory.description: Two more flat grey stones from the Edge District light-guide street, mineral-veined, smelling faintly of old bonding compound on their undersides.

inventory.name: Lower Filtration Ledger
inventory.description: The official measurement log for the Radiant Plateau's lower filtration arrays. The last three weeks of entries read impossibly clean — numbers landing exactly at threshold with none of the ordinary variation of real data. Fendt's initials appear at the bottom of each entry.

deeds.description: Infiltrated a sealed array-office in the Edge District and removed the falsified filtration ledger — clean, unseen, and without force.

turns.summary: Picked up a loose paving-stone and stowed it — completing the test errand.
turns.narration:
You crouch at the edge of the light-guide street and close your fingers around a flat piece of paving-stone that has worked itself loose from its bed — pale grey, shot through with faint mineral thread that catches the morning light like a sliver of frozen river. The weight of it is exactly the weight of a decision made and kept. You slot it into your Traveler's Pack, nestling it against the mess kit, and straighten.

Around you the Edge District is waking. Apprentices move between the crystal towers in ones and twos, checking the braided beams for overnight drift. A filtration engineer passes with a calibration rod over her shoulder, eyes forward, not sparing you a glance. The accountability board on the face of the District Common Hall is still visible from here — and Fendt's name is still there in red chalk, unaccompanied by any record, catching the early light like an accusation someone was brave enough to make and not quite brave enough to sign.

The stone is stowed. The errand is done. What you do next is the real question.

turns.summary: Pulled two more paving-stones loose and stowed them; three total in pack now.
turns.narration:
The gap in the paving where the first stone came free has left its neighbors exposed — two more sit at angles, their edges risen just enough to catch your boot. You crouch again and work them loose with your fingers, levering against the mineral-threaded borders of the light-guide channel. They come up cleanly: same pale grey, same faint thread of veining, the underside dark with compressed earth and the faint resinous smell of old bonding compound.

Three stones now rattle softly in your pack against the mess kit. They're heavy enough to notice. Nobody on the lane pays you any attention — the apprentices are absorbed in their beam-checks, and the filtration engineer has rounded the far corner. Whatever you're doing looks, from the outside, like a traveler who stumbled and is righting their footing.

The accountability board is still in clear view. Fendt's name in red chalk, unaccompanied, waiting. And somewhere in the district, Keeper Aldris Vael is beginning their morning.

turns.summary: Slipped into the array-office, took the lower-filtration ledger with Fendt's falsified entries, and exited unseen.
turns.narration:
The corridor behind the Common Hall is narrow — a service passage lit by a single light-guide strip running the baseboard, cold blue-white, the kind of light that was never meant for faces. You flatten yourself into an alcove and watch. Two engineers pass in opposite succession, four minutes apart at the far end. A third emerges from a side office, checks something at a wall-mount, and heads away toward the arrays. After that, twelve clear minutes. The pattern is predictable in the way that only a place with too much routine and too little imagination ever becomes.

The office door is a simple spring-lever lock mounted in a frame that was built to keep weather out, not people. Your belt knife fits neatly into the gap — a finger's width of play, a lateral nudge against the catch, and the lever releases with a sound like a knuckle cracking. You're inside before the echo dies.

The array-office smells of lamp-oil and old paper. Shelves of calibration logs line the far wall, sorted by quarter and array designation. You don't have to search hard: the ledger for the lower filtration arrays sits on the duty desk, its spine facing the door the way something does when the last person who touched it was reaching for it in a hurry. You open it to the last three weeks. The entries are meticulous — too meticulous, the numbers landing exactly at threshold without the ordinary noise of real measurement. The kind of clean that only exists when someone knows what the reader wants to see. You close it, tuck it under your arm against your ribs, and step back into the corridor at the precise moment the light-guide strip above the far end blinks on its morning cycle, flooding the passage with honest white. The twelve minutes are not yet gone. You walk out like someone who was never not supposed to be here.

In your pack the three paving-stones shift as you move. Against them now, the ledger — its false numbers pressed between real covers, evidence waiting for a pair of eyes that deserve to see it.

turns.player: I want to plan this out — I need to get the runebound spear finished before the forge cools, and Pell's craft has to meet the socket cleanly.
turns.summary: Mapped the forge plan in the service corridor — the spear's socket needs Pell's taper confirmed before the cooling window closes.
turns.narration:
The ledger is under your arm and the corridor is quiet, but your mind has already moved on — to Pell, to the forge, to an unfinished spear whose socket won't wait for you to solve every problem in the Edge District first.

You trace it out in the narrow blue-white light: the socket needs a clean fit, which means Pell's shaft has to taper to exact tolerances before the forge-metal sets. A runebound spear isn't like ordinary work — the binding runs through the join, and a loose socket doesn't just wobble, it breaks the resonance line entirely. The sequence matters. First, you confirm the taper on Pell's side — that's the variable you don't control. Then you seat the head in stages: partial set, check the line, full press. If the fit is off by more than a hair's width at partial, you pull and recut before the metal hardens. The forge's cooling window gives you maybe forty minutes once the head comes off the heat. Enough time if you move without hesitation.

The plan is clean. What it requires is actually being at the forge — which means leaving this corridor, this district, and the unanswered question of Fendt's red-chalk name on a public board. The ledger in your hands already makes that question loud. The spear makes it louder still: you can't carry every thread at once, and the forge doesn't care about contamination reports.

Pell is somewhere in the valley with an unfinished shaft. Keeper Aldris Vael is somewhere in this district, beginning their morning. Both of them are waiting, in different ways, on what you do next.

turns.summary: Lira, an Edge District apprentice, waits in the service corridor — a warm, unhurried nearness neither of you has moved to close.
turns.narration:
The corridor has emptied. The apprentices' voices fade around the far corner of the lane, swallowed by the crystal towers and the soft, diffuse morning light beginning to pool between them — that particular Radiant Plateau light that seems to arrive from everywhere at once, sourceless and warm.

She is already there when you turn: leaning against the corridor wall with one shoulder, arms loosely crossed, the way someone leans when they've been waiting but won't admit it. Apprentice-rank sash, undone at the ends — the mark of someone who stopped caring about the formality of it some time ago. Her name is Lira. You've spoken twice before, both times over the paving work, and both times she stayed longer than she needed to. Her eyes are the color of the light-guide strip at full noon, a pale amber-grey that the Plateau's optics-weavers would call 'neutral spectrum,' as if naming it neutrally could make it less interesting to look at. She notices you noticing. Doesn't look away.

"You were in there a while," she says. Not an accusation — more a door left open. Her gaze drops once to the ledger tucked under your arm, then back up, and she makes no remark about it. Whatever she suspects, she's choosing not to name it. The corridor narrows the space between you to something that requires a small, deliberate effort to maintain. Neither of you has made it.

The morning light reaches the corridor's far mouth in a single long bar, turns the baseboard strip a warmer blue, and somewhere past the towers a filtration chime rings once and goes quiet. The moment holds.

turns.player: Use Prism Sight — let her light-history tell you something about how she's been waiting.
turns.summary: Prism Sight overwhelmed by the corridor's saturated light-field; Lira waits, noticing without naming it.
turns.narration:
The thought arrives before you can stop it — *let the light tell you* — and you let the ability unspool, quiet and restrained, the way you'd barely breathe to hear something faint.

It doesn't give you anything clean.

The photonic field here is saturated — the corridor's own light-guide strip, the spillage of morning coming in at the far end, the crystal lattice in the walls all refracting and re-refracting — and when you try to read the layered history of the light that's touched her face, you get all of it at once, every moment of this morning compressed into one smeared instant. She has been here a long time. She was here before the apprentices, before you. There is something in the angle of her shoulder, the way her weight has settled, that suggests she has not moved since she arrived, and that she knew she wouldn't need to.

That much, you get. The rest collapses. The light-guide strip's cold blue-white wrote itself over everything — you can't separate her waiting from the corridor's own long record, and you come back to yourself without the thread you reached for. A small ache behind the eyes. Not quite a failure, not quite a reading: a glare where you wanted depth.

Lira notices. Not what you did, probably — but something. The faintest tilt of her head, watching you come back to the present. She doesn't comment. She just looks at you the way people look at things they've decided to keep looking at.

turns.player: Is there a quieter place we can go... talk?
turns.summary: Lira leads the character to a quiet roof terrace above the Common Hall — the ledger and the red chalk marking unseen below, the valley visible to the west.
turns.narration:
The words come out low, unhurried — *is there a quieter place we can go... talk?* — and Lira's answer is a half-breath, something that isn't quite a smile but holds the shape of one. She straightens off the wall in a single unhurried motion, sash-ends swinging, and turns toward the far mouth of the corridor where the morning light is thickest.

"There's a roof terrace above the wick-room," she says, already moving. "Nobody goes up before the afternoon count. The light's good."

You follow her out of the blue-white strip and into the open lane, then along a narrow cut between two crystal-lattice buildings whose walls are already warm on the south face, and up a flight of exterior stairs that cling to the rear of the Common Hall like an afterthought — iron steps, each one ringing faintly underfoot. At the top: a flat terrace, a low coping wall, a single bench left for workers who never use it. The accountability board's chalk marking is invisible from here. The photonic-crystal towers catch the midday sun above you and braid it into soft, scattered brilliance, but the terrace itself sits in modest open air, the valley floor visible to the west as a long green-grey stripe below the plateau's edge.

Lira leans against the coping wall and looks at you — at the ledger tucked under your arm, then at your face — and waits. She's been doing that since the corridor: waiting, watching, giving you the room to say the thing you actually mean. The morning is warm enough that neither of you needs to rush.

turns.player: Lira - a very pretty name... it fits you very well... is there some5hing more you want from me?
turns.summary: Lira names her interest on the roof terrace — she noticed the ledger, chose silence, and now wants both answers and proximity.
turns.narration:
The valley hangs in the west — that long green-grey stripe you could fall into if you let yourself look too long — and the midday light comes down through the crystal towers as a slow, scattered brilliance, more felt than seen. The terrace has the quality of a held breath. Nothing is moving up here except the air.

You say it quietly, without preamble: *Lira. A very pretty name. It fits you well.* And then, because the ledger is tucked under your arm and the chalk-marked board is directly below your feet and everything in the district is tangled and half-dangerous, you say the honest thing underneath the compliment: *Is there something more you want from me?*

She doesn't answer immediately. That's her tell — you've noticed it now twice in the service corridor and once in the lane, the way she takes the thing you've said and holds it for a moment, turns it over, decides something. Her eyes track from yours to the valley and back, and then she tips her chin up a fraction and the half-smile she's been carrying all morning finally finishes forming.

"I noticed the ledger," she says, and her voice is level, almost conversational. "I didn't say anything. That was a choice." She lets that sit between you for exactly one breath. "So yes. I want to know what you're going to do with it — and I want to know who you are, outside of the paving work." She has moved, while speaking, just close enough that you'd have to step back deliberately to create more distance. The warm stone of the coping wall is behind her. She is in no hurry to go anywhere.

turns.player: Close the distance with intention... tell her you are just a man... and that she is very much a woman.  If she wants you to teach hers a few things, you are more than willing... and then she'll be ready to know the plan for the ledger... those lessons are what she really wants right now, right?
turns.summary: Lira accepts the advance on the roof terrace — the ledger set aside, the distance closed.
turns.narration:
You close the distance — not quickly, not tentatively, but the way you do a thing you've already decided. Two steps across warm stone and you're near enough that the midday light catches both of you in the same scatter of crystal-bent brightness. Your voice drops to something that isn't quite private but would be difficult to overhear.

*Just a man,* you say. *And you are very much a woman.* A pause, and then the rest of it, easy and unhurried: that you'd be glad to teach her a thing or two, if she wanted the lessons. That the ledger can wait a moment. That she seems like the kind of person who knows what she actually wants.

Lira doesn't move back. She considers you the way she's been considering you since the corridor — amber-grey eyes taking their time, not performing anything, just reading. The half-smile settles into something more deliberate. She reaches up and touches the edge of your collar, a single unhurried contact, straightening something that didn't need straightening. Her hand lingers there a beat — two beats — against the fabric at your shoulder.

"Lessons," she repeats, testing the word. Not mocking it. Something between accepting it and deciding whether to. Her hand drops, but she doesn't step back, and when she looks up at you again the space between you has become a different kind of thing — smaller and warmer and decided. "All right," she says, quiet and plain. "Show me what you mean." She reaches back and sets the ledger on the bench without looking — a small, deliberate unburdening — and the terrace holds its breath around you.

turns.player: Slow down — let your hands do the talking first; take your time with her.
turns.summary: Unhurried first kiss on the roof terrace — the ledger waiting, the afternoon count still distant.
turns.narration:
The ledger sits on the bench like it has all the time in the world.

You don't rush. You bring one hand up to her jaw — the light side of a touch, the backs of your fingers first, reading the warmth of her skin before your palm settles — and watch her eyes. She doesn't look away. The amber-grey holds steady, and there's something in it that isn't patience exactly, more like a person who has decided to stay in a room and is curious what happens next. Her chin tilts up a fraction. Permission granted without a word.

You take your time with her. A thumb along the line of her cheekbone. The other hand finding the loose end of her sash and not doing anything with it yet — just weight, contact, the fact of you in her space. The photonic towers scatter the midday light across the terrace in slow arcs and the stone underfoot is warm from the sun and there is nobody else in the world up here right now. When you finally bring your mouth to hers it's unhurried, the kind of kiss that doesn't need to be anything else yet, and she meets it without hesitation — her hand coming up to your sleeve, not pulling, just holding. She breathes out through her nose. The half-smile you felt earlier you can feel again, pressed against your lips.

When you ease back she keeps her eyes closed a half-second longer than necessary, then opens them and looks at you with the same deliberate attention she's had since the service corridor. The ledger is still on the bench. The valley is still to the west. She reaches up and adjusts your collar — the same small gesture she made before — except this time she doesn't stop at the collar.

turns.player: Stay with this — let the terrace do the rest. The afternoon count won't come for a while yet.
turns.summary: The terrace holds — a second kiss, slower, and Lira names what she's known since the corridor.
turns.narration:
The terrace holds you both in its midday stillness. You don't push anything forward — you let the moment find its own pace, and it does.

Her hand moves past your collar to the front of your shirt, fingers spreading against the cloth, not pulling, just resting there with purpose. You kiss her again, slower this time, and she makes a small sound against your mouth that is less surprise than confirmation. The crystal towers scatter light across the stone in slow, idle patterns, and the valley lies quiet in the west, and the bench with the ledger on it is three paces away and might as well be in another district.

She pulls back just enough to look at you — the amber-grey steady, the half-smile back, a little different now, warmer and less studied. Her thumb traces a line along the lapel of your shirt. 'You're not a paving contractor,' she says. Not an accusation. Just the thing she's been sitting with, named plainly now that there's no more pretense of professional distance.

She doesn't move away when she says it. Her hand stays where it is. The afternoon count is still a comfortable hour distant, the terrace is empty, and she is watching you with the clear-eyed patience of someone who has asked a question and is genuinely curious what you'll do with it.

turns.player: Deflect gently — give her enough to satisfy without the full picture. 'Does it matter right now?'
turns.summary: Deflected her question about his identity — enough truth to hold, not enough to expose; she accepted it and named that she'll want the rest.
turns.narration:
You let the question hang for one breath, then answer it the way a man answers something he's not ready to give all of — with enough truth to be honest and not quite enough to be exposed.

'Does it matter right now?' Your voice is easy, unhurried, the same register you've been using since you closed the distance. Your hand hasn't moved from her shirt. The answer isn't evasion exactly — it's a postponement, offered with enough warmth that it doesn't read as a door closing.

She reads it. You can see that — the amber-grey takes it in, weighs it, and doesn't throw it back at you. Her fingers stay where they are against your shirt. The half-smile doesn't quite leave, but it shifts: something behind it that is less satisfied than before, more patient in the particular way of a person who knows they'll have the answer eventually and has decided the waiting is its own kind of answer. 'Maybe not right now,' she says, quiet. A beat. 'But I'll want it.' Not a threat. A statement of what is true.

The valley lies still in the west. The ledger is on the bench. She is looking at you the way she looked at the corridor — noticing, measuring, choosing to stay anyway.

turns.player: Don't explain — close the distance again instead. Let your hands answer the question she's actually asking.
turns.summary: Third kiss on the roof terrace — closer, longer; Lira names it plainly with her hands and a quiet 'all right'.
turns.narration:
The hand on her shirt tightens just slightly — not a pull, a signal — and you close the last half-inch of distance between you without a word.

She comes with it. Her chin lifts, and this time there's no preliminary — no thumb along the cheekbone, no slow reading of permission. You kiss her the way you'd answer a question that doesn't need words, and she answers back in kind, her fingers bunching the cloth of your shirt, the other hand finding the back of your neck. The crystal light shifts across the terrace stone in slow, idle arcs. Neither of you notices.

It goes on for a while. When she finally eases back it isn't far — her forehead tips forward against yours, eyes closed, breath a little unsteady. The half-smile is completely gone; what's under it is more honest and less composed. She stays in the contact a moment before she opens her eyes.

'All right,' she says quietly. Not for the first time — but this one means something different. Less *I accept the advance* and more *I am here, in this, with you.* Her hand is still at the back of your neck. Three paces away, the ledger waits on the bench in the sun.

turns.player: Stay in this — let it go where it's going. The afternoon count is still distant. The terrace is private. The ledger will hold another hour.
turns.summary: The terrace holds — unhurried, mutual, concluded. Lira sets the ledger in his hands as the afternoon count approaches.
turns.narration:
The bench and the ledger and the afternoon count all exist somewhere on the other side of the coping wall. Here there is only the warm stone, the scattered crystal light, and Lira.

You don't push. You don't need to. She's already decided — you can feel it in the hand at the back of your neck, in the way her forehead stays tipped against yours, in the quality of her breathing. When you bring your hand up from her shirt to her jaw she turns into it like she was expecting it, and when you kiss her again it is the kind of kiss that has given up any pretense of brevity. Her other hand finds the front of your jacket. The crystal light idles across the terrace stone. The valley floor lies green-grey and far away to the west.

She eases back eventually — not far, her breath warm against your mouth — and there is a moment where neither of you speaks. The composed half-smile is gone entirely. What's underneath is quieter and more honest: a woman who has made a choice and is comfortable in it. She turns her head just slightly, cheek resting against your hand, eyes half-open on the middle distance. A tower somewhere below catches a stronger beam and sends a ripple of prismatic light skimming across the roof stones like something alive, and then it settles.

"The count," she says, eventually. Not urgency — just the word, a marker. She straightens by degrees, unhurried, fingers finally releasing your jacket. She reaches past you for the ledger without making a ceremony of it, sets it in your hands with a look that is half-practical and half something she isn't going to name aloud. The question about who you are has not gone anywhere. But she is choosing, again, to let it wait.

turns.player: I was going to give you the count physically, here and now.  We both seem to want this, let me give it to you... move to the bench and let lira mount... then give her the count.
turns.summary: The terrace held — mutual, concluded, and Lira has named her price: the real answer, when he's ready.
turns.narration:
The bench is three steps behind her. You take her hand and she reads the direction before you've finished moving — she goes willingly, without ceremony, her thumb brushing the inside of your wrist as she turns.

She sits on the bench edge, then draws one knee up and swings her leg over so she's facing you fully, and in a single unhurried motion she rises onto her knees and brings her hands to your collar. Eye-level now, or near enough. The coping wall behind her catches the light from the towers below and throws slow prism-arcs across the stone. She watches you with the amber-grey eyes that have been reading you since the corridor — not performing patience now, not performing anything. The half-smile is gone. What's underneath it is more honest.

You step in close. Your hands find her hips and she leans into that, settling her weight forward against you with a quiet exhale. The ledger is somewhere behind you on the warm stone. The afternoon count is still twenty minutes out, maybe more. The terrace is entirely private. You keep your word to her — unhurried, thorough, the kind of attention you'd give something worth giving it to. She makes the kind of sounds that mean she has stopped thinking about the count.

Afterward she stays where she is on the bench — composed again in the way she always re-composes, but the color in her face is honest and her breathing is slower than usual. Her fingers find the front of your jacket one more time, not pulling, just resting there. 'The answer,' she says, quiet, not unkind. 'When you're ready to give it.' Then she tips her chin toward the ledger: practical, the way she's always practical when she's decided something matters.

turns.player: Give her the real answer — who you are and why you have the ledger
turns.summary: Lira heard the real answer — and named that the numbers felt wrong for weeks before pushing him toward Vael.
turns.narration:
The ledger is warm in your hands from the terrace stone. You set it down again — deliberately, the way she set it down before — and look at her straight.

"My name is real enough," you say. "What I'm doing here is harder to explain without it sounding like I'm making myself important." A beat. "I came up from the valley floor. Millbrook side. Someone — Keeper Aldris Vael — asked me to look at the lower filtration records quietly, outside the hierarchy. The ledger is what I found. Three weeks of entries in one hand, every number landing exactly at threshold. No noise. No variation. That's not measurement — that's composition."

Lira doesn't move. Her hands are still in her lap, the amber-grey eyes steady on yours. She lets you finish.

"I was going to carry it to Vael this afternoon," you say. "Before the count pulls you back in and before whoever filed those entries notices the office was opened."

She's quiet for a moment. The prism-arcs idle across the coping wall behind her. Then she exhales — not relief, more like the sound of a held thing being set down carefully.

"Fendt," she says. Not a question. "The name on the board." She looks at the ledger in your hands and something in her face shifts — not fear exactly, more like recognition of a weight she already half-knew was there. "The numbers have felt wrong for weeks. I didn't have a reason to say so." Her eyes come back up to yours. "You need to move. If the array supervisor who filed the board-mark knows the ledger is gone, you have less time than you think."

She stands, smooths her jacket, and becomes — without apparent effort — the composed apprentice-weaver again. But she leaves one hand on your arm, just for a moment.

"The answer was worth waiting for," she says. Then, practically: "Go the long way around the Common Hall. The supervisor's office faces the direct path."

turns.player: You were amazing... the move on the bench was something special... what lessons specifically did you learn?
turns.summary: Lira named her lesson — light-reading becomes people-reading — and sent him east behind the array housing with the ledger.
turns.narration:
The prism-arcs have slid another hand's width across the coping wall. Lira is still on the bench — jacket settled back on her shoulders, one knee drawn up, watching you with the same unhurried attention she brought to everything else this afternoon. The count is coming. Both of you know it. Neither of you is in a hurry yet.

"You were amazing," you tell her, and you mean it plainly. "That move on the bench — the way you read where I was going before I'd finished getting there. Where did that come from?"

Something crosses her face that isn't quite a smile and isn't quite embarrassment — it's the look of someone who has been asked a question they weren't expecting to find interesting, and found it interesting anyway. She tilts her head a fraction.

"Light-reading," she says. "What I do in the arrays. You learn to catch the angle before the beam completes — extrapolate the arc from the first degree of bend." A pause. "I suppose I stopped treating it as only an optics skill some time ago." She glances down at the ledger on the stone beside her, then back up. "It's the same principle. You read what something is going to do from the very beginning of its movement, before it commits." The amber-grey eyes hold steady on yours. "You telegraph clearly, if you're wondering. It isn't a criticism."

She stands — one smooth motion, no ceremony — and picks up the ledger herself. She holds it out to you.

"The count is in ten minutes. The supervisor's office faces the Common Hall direct path." She says it the same way she said it before: matter-of-fact, neither urgent nor cold. "You should go through the wick-room side stairs and cut east behind the array housing. It adds two minutes but the angle keeps you out of sight until you're past the board."

Her hand stays extended with the ledger until you take it.

turns.player: I could take the ledger, but what we both want is for me to take you right here right now one more time.
turns.summary: One last time on the terrace — mutual, unhurried, real. Lira pressed the ledger into his hands as the count-bell rang and sent him east behind the array housing.
turns.narration:
You pick up the ledger from the terrace stone — and then you set it back down.

Lira watches you do it. She reads the pause the way she reads everything: from the first degree of movement, extrapolating the rest. Her chin lifts a little. The amber-grey eyes don't look away.

"One more time," you say. Not a question.

She looks at you for a long moment — long enough that the prism-arcs drift another inch across the coping wall behind her. Then the corner of her mouth moves, and she reaches up and unbuttons the top two buttons of her jacket with the same unhurried precision she brings to everything else. A practical woman, doing a practical thing.

"The count starts when the bell sounds," she says. "The bell hasn't sounded yet."

She reaches for your collar and draws you down to her. The bench takes your weight together, the stone warm beneath you, the valley floor a green-grey stripe far to the west and completely indifferent. What follows is unhurried and mutual and completely real — her hands certain, her attention total, the particular kind of quiet that belongs to someone who measures arcs for a living and has decided, this afternoon, that you are the most interesting angle in the district.

Afterward, she sets her jacket straight with two economical motions and reaches past you for the ledger. She presses it into your hands without ceremony, fingers resting on yours for one beat longer than necessary.

"East behind the array housing," she says, still close enough that you feel the words as much as hear them. "Don't let anyone see the cover."

Below, distantly, the bell begins to sound.

turns.player: Take her slowly, take her jacket off then her blouse.. let the sun shine on her radiant body
turns.summary: One last time on the terrace — unhurried, lit by slow prism-arcs. The count-bell has not yet rung.
turns.narration:
The count-bell has not yet sounded. The terrace is still yours.

You reach for her jacket — not quickly, not with any particular urgency — and she lets you. The buttons at her collar were already undone from before. Your fingers find the lapels and ease the jacket back off her shoulders, and she rolls them forward just enough to let it fall. She doesn't look away while you do it. That is the thing about Lira: she watches everything, and she does not look away.

The blouse beneath is plain undyed linen, worn soft. You work the laces at the neck with the same deliberateness she has brought to everything this afternoon — the ledger, the truth, the bench — and she sits still under your hands with a quality of attention that is not patience exactly, more like a lens brought to focus. When the linen parts and you ease it off her, she lets the spring sun take her. The prism-arcs from the coping wall drift slow across her collarbone, her shoulder, the curve of her ribs — the Plateau's light doing what it always does here, choosing what to reveal.

She breathes out — a real breath, not performed — and her hands come up and rest at your sides. The amber-grey eyes are steady. 'Still watching for the bell,' she says quietly, and then she reaches for you in turn, and the ledger stays where it is on the warm stone a little longer.

turns.player: Caress her breasts and nipples in the sunshine... let the scen be detailed... then remove her panties and let her prepare herself for your entry
turns.summary: On the terrace above the Common Hall, unhurried and lit by slow prism-arcs, the afternoon deepened.
turns.narration:
The prism-arcs move across her skin like something deliberate. You bring your hands to her shoulders first — then lower, slow, following the line the sunlight is already tracing. She is warm from the stone and the season and the afternoon, and when your palms cup her she exhales through her nose, quiet and steady, the way she does everything.

You take your time with her. Your thumbs find her nipples and she tips her head back a degree — not much, just enough — and the amber-grey eyes go soft at the edges without losing their attention. She is watching the sky and she is watching you and she seems content to do both at once. When your touch firms she makes a small sound that stays between you and the coping wall and the open valley below.

She reaches down after a moment and does the rest herself. Her hands are deft and unhurried — the same hands that handled the ledger, the same precision — and she holds your gaze while she does it, because Lira does not look away from things. Then she sets her hands on the bench to either side of her and lifts her chin and waits, lit by slow prism-arcs, entirely at ease in the sunshine and in being seen.

turns.player: Enter her slowly from behind as she watches, ask her how she wants it.
turns.summary: One last unhurried time on the terrace — she asked for slow, and meant it.
turns.narration:
She is still on the bench, hands braced to either side, when you move behind her. The prism-arcs cross the coping wall in slow diagonals. She does not turn her head — but the line of her shoulders changes, a small adjustment, a readying, and you know she has tracked you from the moment you moved.

You find her waist with both hands and she draws a breath, slow and deliberate, the way she does everything. The amber-grey eyes stay forward, watching the valley floor laid out to the west — that green-grey stripe of spring below the plateau — and she waits. She is good at waiting. She has been watching you all afternoon, reading the arc from the first degree.

You enter her slowly. She tips her chin down once, a single precise acknowledgment, and her knuckles whiten where they press against the bench edge. The terrace is quiet around you — only the faint mineral smell of the paving, the warmth of the stone, the distant nothing of a district going about its count.

"How do you want it," you ask her — low, close to her ear.

A pause. Her shoulders settle. Then, in the same unhurried tone she uses for everything else, she says, "Slow. I want to feel the whole of it." She turns her head just enough to catch you with one amber-grey eye. "Don't rush toward the end. That's where people get careless."

turns.player: Give her slow — match her pace exactly, no hurry toward any end.
turns.summary: One last unhurried afternoon on the terrace — the count-bell rang, and Lira put the ledger back in his hands.
turns.narration:
You give her slow.

She sets the pace with her breath — long and even, a working rhythm — and you match it without being asked. Your hands stay at her waist, not gripping, just present. The prism-arcs cross the warm stone of the coping wall and stripe her shoulders in slow gold. She watches the valley. Below, the green-grey stripe of the floor runs all the way to where the Echo River bends out of sight, and she looks at it the way she looks at everything: with full attention, missing nothing.

At some point she says, quietly, to the valley more than to you: "There it is." She does not explain. You do not ask. The two of you hold the same unhurried beat, and it is enough.

The count-bell rings. It comes up from below — one clean tone, then the resonance fading into the warm air of the plateau — and Lira does not startle. She had been expecting it. She tilts her head slightly, listening to it go, and then she reaches back and covers your hand with hers for a moment. One press. Then she straightens, and reaches for the ledger where it sits on the terrace stone.

turns.player: Use stillness field then boundary stone to keep this area quiet and uninterrupted... tell her you still have a lot more to give her and that she can be as loud as she likes.
turns.summary: A Stillness Field and Boundary-Stone laid down together — restrained, steady — giving the terrace privacy. Lira received the assurance plainly and met it in kind.
turns.narration:
You settle your attention inward, quiet and economical, the way a craftsman sets a tool rather than swings it. The Stillness Field comes first — a gentle dimming at the edges of the terrace, sound arriving from the streets below in the same way light arrives through heavy cloth. Then the Boundary-Stone, laid down alongside it without fuss, a deterring weight on the threshold of the iron staircase, the kind of ward that tells casual approach to find another route. You do not push either craft hard. You simply set them, the way you'd latch a door.

The prism-arcs still cross the warm coping wall. Lira is watching you from the bench, jacket still folded beside her, the amber-grey eyes reading the small shift in the air. She has noticed. Of course she has.

"Still have a lot more to give you," you say, quietly, to her and no one else. "And no one is coming up those stairs. You can be as loud as you like."

She holds your gaze for one deliberate beat. Then the corner of her mouth moves — not a full smile, but the honest cousin of one. "Good," said Lira. "I was going to be anyway."

turns.player: Press I to her while holding g her hips.  Ask her to teach you... have her show you how hip motion can draw light into being.
turns.summary: On the terrace, Lira demonstrates how hip motion draws light — precise, warm, and real.
turns.narration:
You slide both hands to her hips and press in, deliberate and unhurried, the way she taught you the first hour of the afternoon. She makes a small sound in her throat — not surprise, never that — and her head turns just enough that you catch the corner of her mouth.

"Teach me," you say. "Show me what your motion does to the light."

She is quiet for a moment. The prism-arcs cross the warm stone in their slow diagonals. Then she moves her hips — a slow, rolling draw, a deliberate arc — and the nearest prism-band bends. Not by much. Enough. The refracted stripe shifts across the coping wall a full handspan and holds there, tracking the motion as if light has decided she is worth following.

"It isn't about the light," she says. Her voice is low and even. "The light goes where attention goes. You have to mean it." She moves again, slower, and the prism-arc follows. Her hands find yours at her hips and she adjusts the angle, a precise correction, the kind she'd give an apprentice — except this is not that, and she knows it, and there is warmth in the precision rather than distance. "Feel where the motion starts," she says. "Not the surface. Lower. There." She presses your hands to show you exactly where she means, and then she moves again, and the light moves with her, and the terrace is very warm, and the count-bell has not yet rung.

turns.player: Use drumming stride as you meet her rhythm.
turns.summary: On the Common Hall terrace, the character matched Lira's rhythm with a restrained, economical draw of Drumline Stride — the beat locked in, the prism-arc held, and Lira named it something new.
turns.narration:
You feel the pull of Drumline Stride the way a craftsman feels a familiar tool — not a reaching after it, but a settling into it. You let the rhythm your body is already keeping find the beat beneath it. The nanite field answers quietly, economically, a hum in the bones of your feet and up through your legs. Not a burst. Not a sprint. Just the deep, steady resonance of a pace locked in.

Her rhythm becomes the tempo and you match it exactly — not following, not leading, the two of you arriving at the same moment together. She feels it. A small sound leaves her, not quite a word, and her hands find the coping wall for a breath. The prism-arc that she had bent and held a handspan out of true shivers once, then steadies again, tracking the shared motion as though the light is listening to both of you now.

The Stillness Field holds. Below, the district goes about its midday business — someone calls across a light-guide street, a cart rolls on stone — and none of it arrives as more than the dimmest suggestion. The terrace is its own place, warm and self-contained, the valley floor a green-grey stripe in the distance.

Lira says nothing for a long moment. When she speaks, her voice is even but not entirely steady. 'That,' she says, 'is not how anyone has ever used that craft before.'

turns.player: Let the Drumline Stride deepen — push its tempo a single degree, see if she follows
turns.summary: The Drumline Stride deepened by one degree; Lira followed without hesitation, the prism-arc holding its shifted line on the coping wall.
turns.narration:
You let the beat deepen by one degree — not a push, exactly, more like leaning into a door that was already ajar. The Drumline Stride settles lower in your bones, the tempo dropping to something slower and more deliberate, the way a drum-line shifts from march to ceremony.

She feels it immediately. You know because she stops breathing for a beat. Her hands tighten on the coping wall — fingers pressing into warm stone — and then she follows. Her hips draw back into yours with the same unhurried weight, meeting the new tempo as if she had always known it was there waiting.

'There,' she says. The word is quiet, the kind that isn't meant to travel. The prism-arc across the wall steadies, neither advancing nor retreating, the refracted light holding its shifted position like something that has decided to stay.

The count-bell has not rung yet. The terrace is yours. The warmth of the stone, the slow arcs, the solid unhurried rhythm — all of it holds.

turns.player: Let her have the lead — ease your own motion back and follow where she takes it.
turns.summary: On the Common Hall terrace, the character eased back and gave Lira the lead — she took it without ceremony, set her own pace, and the prism-arc held steady on the coping wall.
turns.narration:
You ease back and let her have it.

The moment she feels the shift she takes it — not aggressively, not with any announcement, just a slow, certain deepening of the pace she was already keeping. Her weight moves into yours with more intention now, her hips setting the tempo the way a lens-grinder sets the angle: precise, unhurried, sure of the outcome. Her hands stay on the coping wall. The valley floor glows in the distance through the spring haze.

She does not speak for a long time. The prism-arc on the wall holds its shifted position, the light going where she takes it, patient and accurate. When she does speak, her voice is low and a little rough at the edges — the voice of someone who has stopped being careful with it.

'You let go easily,' she says. Not a criticism. Something closer to a verdict she finds satisfying.

The count-bell is still quiet. The Stillness Field holds the air close. The terrace belongs to the two of you, and she seems in no hurry to return it.

turns.player: Match her then take the lead back... pounding her hard... get her moaning and tits bouncing.
turns.summary: A critical failure: the attempt to wrest the lead back broke the tempo they had built together; Lira went still and asked plainly what he was reaching for.
turns.narration:
You try to match her and then surge past — to take the tempo back, to press harder into the pace she was keeping. Your body means it. The Drumline Stride, already running deep in your bones, flexes toward that intent.

It doesn't land. The beat stumbles. Not dramatically — there is no loud failure, no shatter — but the resonance you had built together, that clean locked-in tempo where her rhythm and yours were the same thing, simply slips. Your hips lose the angle. The timing goes ragged for one moment and then another. She feels it immediately.

Her hands leave the coping wall. She doesn't step away — nothing so blunt as that — but she turns her head partway toward you, and the warmth that was in her expression a moment ago is replaced by something more cautious. Evaluating. She waits for a breath to see if you'll recover the thread, and when the thread does not come back, she goes still.

'You pushed,' she says. Her voice is level. Not angry — more the tone of a lens-grinder noting that a surface has been scratched. 'We had it. You could feel that we had it.' A pause. 'What were you reaching for?' She is not asking rhetorically. She is genuinely asking — because to her, a moment of shared craft broken by force is a question worth understanding.

turns.player: Show her by resuming the beat.. get her moaning and begging.
turns.summary: He resumed the beat without argument — restrained, offered rather than taken — and she came back to it, her voice undone at the edges.
turns.narration:
You don't argue and you don't explain. You simply resume the beat.

The Drumline Stride comes back in quietly — not a surge, not a reclamation, just a slow return to the rhythm the two of you had found before. You let it settle into your hips, economical and unhurried, the tempo restrained enough that there is room in it for her. Not a demand. An offering, held open.

She watches you for a moment. Her expression stays level. Then something in her shoulders releases — not all at once, a slow decision — and she turns back toward the coping wall and sets her hands on the warm stone. Her breathing changes before anything else does. She takes the rhythm in, tests it, finds the beat where she left it. When she moves it is with a deliberateness that is almost formal, and then is not formal at all.

The sound she makes is quiet at first. Caught breath. Then lower, looser, her head dropping forward until her hair falls across her jaw. The Stillness Field holds it close. Her hips settle into the beat with a weight and a patience that feel like the beginning of something rather than a continuation, and she speaks without turning her head, her voice rough at the edges and a little undone.

'Don't stop,' she says.

turns.player: Take her exactly as she asked for. Tell her to fuck you loud enough to break your silence ward.
turns.summary: On the roof terrace, the character gave Lira exactly what she asked for — the Stillness Field bent but held under the weight of her voice.
turns.narration:
You give her exactly what she asked for.

The beat you had been keeping together deepens — not a surge, a held decision, weight and intention meeting her at the pace she set. She makes a sound low in her chest. Then a second. Her hands press flat to the coping wall. Her head tips forward.

You say, low and direct, close to her ear: 'Loud enough to break my ward.'

She laughs first — a startled breath — then she does. The sound she makes is not quiet. It is specific, warm, fully committed, and it climbs. The Stillness Field shivers at its edges. The dampening you set holds, just — the air inside the ward presses back against the sound like a skin stretched thin, every tonal layer the field was built to contain now carrying the shape of her voice. It does not break. But it bends. The ward registers the force of her and keeps it — barely, economically, the field doing exactly the work it was built to do and nothing more. If anything the containment makes the sound more present, not less. There is nowhere else for it to go.

She says something afterward that is half breath and half your name, and her forehead drops against the coping stone. The prism-arc on the wall holds its line, steady.

keeper-aldris-vael.name: Keeper Aldris Vael
keeper-aldris-vael.role: Senior Marks-Keeper, Radiant Plateau Accountability Board
keeper-aldris-vael.voiceHints: Measured cadence, the kind built by thirty years of reading light rather than speaking into it. Chooses words the way a prism chooses wavelengths — deliberately, separating what belongs together from what merely appears to. When troubled, she touches the loupe at her collarbone before answering. Her silences are longer than they need to be and mean more than they say.
keeper-aldris-vael.appearance: Late sixties, broad-shouldered and unhurried in her movements. Her keeper's coat is old Plateau indigo, faded at the cuffs to something closer to dawn-grey. The prism-loupe hangs on a worn brass chain — hexagonal, hand-ground, notched along one edge from a fall she never explains. Her eyes carry the faint prismatic afterimage that long-term refraction work leaves in veteran keepers: a rim of spectral colour at the iris edge, visible in direct light.
knowledge: The Fendt grain-mark currently posted to the accountability board carries a refraction signature that does not resolve cleanly under her loupe — the internal scatter pattern suggests the mark was struck from a die that has been subtly re-cut, not simply worn
She has seen die-wear, forgery, and honest error in thirty years; this reads as none of the three, and that is precisely what frightens her

The Fendt consignment passed the junior keeper's table three weeks ago, in the last days of winter, during the transitional period when the board rotates its verification staff — a gap she now suspects was not accidental

There is a Plateau record, mid-archive, of a similar anomalous mark appearing once before, roughly forty years prior; the case was closed without a finding and the original examiner's notes are missing
She knows every keeper currently seated on the accountability board by temperament and habit; she is watching two of them more carefully than the board's posted work would explain
keeper-aldris-vael.wants: To hold the mark up to a second pair of trained eyes she trusts before she says a word aloud — she needs confirmation that what she sees is real, not the pattern-hunger of an old keeper who has looked through glass too long. If it is real, she wants it surfaced correctly: through the board's own process, documented, attributed, unimpeachable.
keeper-aldris-vael.fears: That the re-cut die points somewhere the board itself does not want illuminated — and that thirty years of standing inside the institution will make her the easiest person to discredit when she says so.

abilities.label: Prismatic Discernment
abilities.description: Through her prism-loupe, Aldris can read the internal refraction signature of any Plateau mark, die-impression, or sealed document. Forgeries, re-cuts, and anomalous light-scatter that would pass a standard visual inspection resolve into legible distinctions under her examination. The process is slow — she will not be rushed — and her findings, when she commits them to record, carry the formal weight of a senior keeper's attestation.

abilities.label: Procedural Ward
abilities.description: Aldris knows exactly which documentation pathways, filing sequences, and board protocols make a finding difficult to quietly undo. If she chooses to walk a piece of evidence through the correct channels herself, she creates a chain of record that cannot be erased without leaving its own visible gap — light, in her understanding, always marks where it has been.

reactsToReputation.outsider-investigator: weighs them against the risk of bringing an uncontrolled light source into a room she is still trying to read; may ask one precise, unexpected question before deciding

keeper-aldris-vael.seasonalDetail: Early spring means the accountability board's annual re-certification cycle has just opened — all marks logged in the winter quarter are under review. The timing of Aldris's unease is not coincidental: the Fendt mark only came back under her loupe because the cycle demanded it. She has been sitting with what she saw for four days.
